summary:
Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, expressly including sexual orientation and gender identity, within a secular, multinational order. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1997, when Constitutional Tribunal Case No. 111-97-TC struck Article 516 of the Penal Code, and the 1998 Constitution made Ecuador the first country in the Americas to bar discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-determination. The 2016 Gender Identity Law allows a change of legal gender and birth name on identity documents without surgery or medical diagnosis. The National Assembly's reforms of 12 December 2023 to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data were followed by the reglamento that President Noboa issued on 11 June 2024, which streamlines the civil-registry procedure through which marker changes are carried out.

Rulings reported by AP in April 2026 let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records, in a case described as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states that legal gender recognition is not available to people under 18, so the reach of the April 2026 rulings for minors is not settled in this record.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019. Adoption is limited to different-sex couples under Article 68 of the Constitution, and on 14 August 2026 new adoption legislation passed 118-0 explicitly prohibiting single and same-sex couples from adopting. In May 2018 the Constitutional Court ordered the Civil Registry to register the daughter of the same-sex couple Helen Bicknell and Nicola Rothon, the child Satya Amani Bicknell Rothon, by 5-3 with one abstention; lawyer Jose Luis Guerra said the refusal had violated the child's rights. A trans visitor whose relationship would be classed locally as same-sex can marry, and faces the same adoption bar as any locally same-sex couple.

Conversion practices are criminalised. Article 151 of the Penal Code, added in 2014, treats conversion therapy as equivalent to torture and carries 7 to 10 years' imprisonment, and Outright International records that conversion practices involving torture are explicitly criminalised. As of 2023, hundreds of clinics were still promoting the practice.

Los Angeles Blade reported in January 2024 that violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians is increasing amid the country's internal armed conflict. The U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report recorded discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, found that gay, lesbian and transgender people suffered discrimination from public and private bodies, found that the right to equal access to formal education was frequently violated, and reported LGBT groups' claims that police and prosecutors did not thoroughly investigate deaths of LGBT individuals. The most recent official country report in this record dates from 2011.

Detention carries a specific and documented exposure. Trans women are held in Ecuador's almost universally male prisons, in male spaces, and Silueta X's PrisioTrans documentation covering 2011 to 2026 records gender-identity discrimination, unsafe placement, sexual violence, forced suppression of gender expression and barriers to health care. Trans woman Helen Maldonado died during the November 2021 massacre at Penitenciaria del Litoral while held in a male prison space; a 2022 complaint alleged cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of trans women in Lago Agrio; 2024 allegations concerned forced head-shaving, beatings and violence targeting breast and body implants; and the 2026 death in State custody of a 23-year-old trans woman at the El Encuentro maximum-security prison drew calls for an independent investigation.
tangentialFactors:
Ecuador's constitutional protection and its legislature have moved in opposite directions. The 1998 Constitution made the country the first in the Americas to bar sexual-orientation discrimination, while the adoption statute passed on 14 August 2026 by 118-0 explicitly excluded single and same-sex couples from adopting.

The social climate described in the sources is conservative. The 2011 human rights report characterised a macho culture in which homosexuality tends to be viewed negatively, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption as societal problems. Against that, pride marches have been authorised in all major cities with police protection and official participation: the first was held in Quito in 1998; the 2011 Guayaquil march included a vice prefect, a city councillor and a National Assembly member; attendance reached about 20,000 in Guayaquil in 2017, when the Bolívar and San Martín monuments were lit in rainbow colours, and over 18,000 in Quito in 2018; the Presidential House was lit in rainbow colours in June 2017.

Public hostility from office-holders has been penalised. In 2013 a presidential candidate, Nelson Zavala, was fined over $3,000 and barred from office for a year for calling gay people 'sinners' and 'immoral'.

Two structural factors raise the level of ambient risk. The January 2024 reporting ties rising violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians to an internal armed conflict, which is a general-turmoil condition rather than a trans-specific legal one, and the carceral exposure described by Silueta X and the Pulitzer Center is driven by a prison system that operates almost entirely on male lines.
localsOnly:
Prison placement operates by birth sex or legal sex. The Pulitzer Center investigation found that Ecuador's prisons are almost always male, that trans women are placed in male pavilions, and that protective placement in the 'prioritaria' pavilion reserved for vulnerable populations, where many sexo-gender-diverse inmates are held, is used unevenly. In August 2023 Alexa, a 27-year-old Venezuelan trans woman detained at Penitenciaria del Litoral, was sent to male pavilion 9 with three other trans women rather than the prioritaria pavilion, and she received no medical exams or HIV treatment there. The investigation documents rapes and torture reported to be directed at prisoners' gender identity.

The last prison census counted 73 trans women across all Ecuadorian prisons, a raw count without a denominator or a stated census year; the organisation Fundacion Vivir Libre says the true number is many higher.

Silueta X does not press a single placement rule. Its PrisioTrans program advocates individualised housing decisions under regional human-rights standards, weighing gender identity, safety, the detainee's own assessment and informed consent, and it cites the July 2016 government decision to develop protocols for LGBT people deprived of liberty.

Trans people have held elected and candidacies-level office: Diane Marie Rodríguez Zambrano became the first openly transgender candidate in 2013 and the first transgender lawmaker in 2017.

Resident-facing welfare findings in the record are dated. The 2011 report found that gay, lesbian and transgender people's right to equal access to formal education was frequently violated, and that clinics had confined young people against their will, including the daughter of parents who unsuccessfully sought her release.
outOfScopeNotes:
The availability of legal gender recognition for under-18s is unresolved between two sources. Outright International's overview, updated 12 March 2026, says recognition is not available to under-18s, while AP reported in April 2026 that Constitutional Court rulings let trans adolescents change name and sex on official records. Whether the 2024 reglamento applies to minors is not stated in this inventory.

No trans-specific violence figure with a denominator appears in this record. The January 2024 report that violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians is increasing supplies no count, no period total and no general homicide comparison, so the magnitude of that increase cannot be established here, and no later quantified assessment is sourced.

The 73-trans-woman prison census figure carries no census year, no total prison population and no per-capita basis, and the source itself says the number is undercounted; it should not be read as a measure of risk.

Findings on police investigation of LGBT deaths, education access and discrimination by public and private bodies come from a 2011 report. Whether later official monitoring exists is not sourced here.

The count of clinics still promoting conversion practices as of 2023 has no update in this inventory, so current levels of that practice are not documented.
